query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching the deposition process from the current thermal-spray method to a High‐Velocity Oxygen Fuel (HVOF) system with optimized parameters (e.g., increased particle velocity and reduced in-flight residence time) will enable the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat to achieve a thicker deposit than the current 15–45 μm feedstock baseline while preserving coating integrity and minimizing as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat produced from 15–45 μm feedstock, which currently yields an insufficient coating thickness.
generation.intervention: Implement HVOF deposition by adjusting process parameters (e.g., higher particle kinetic energy via increased oxygen/fuel flow and reduced spray distance) to boost deposition efficiency.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed on the usual substrate under ambient atmospheric conditions using HVOF, with process settings chosen to keep particle exposure to oxidizing environments minimal. The intervention is intended to work under standard thermal barrier coating system service conditions where high temperature and oxidation resistance are required.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle momentum promotes better flattening and splat coalescence leading to increased build-up of coating thickness, while the shorter in-flight time reduces oxidation of the feedstock particles.
generation.mechanism: The higher velocity of the particles in the HVOF process increases the deposition efficiency by promoting denser, more cohesive splat formation. Simultaneously, the decreased residence time in an oxidizing atmosphere limits the extent of in-flight oxidation, thus preserving the intended microstructural integrity and preventing excessive oxide formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coating thickness will be increased by a significant margin (i.e., a statistically measurable improvement over the baseline 15–45 μm range) without an accompanying rise in oxidation levels as compared to the current deposition method.
generation.baseline: Thermal-spray deposition from 15–45 μm feedstock that produces a bond coat with insufficient thickness but acceptable minimal oxidation levels.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective provided that the HVOF parameters (e.g., particle velocity, spray distance, and feedstock characteristics) are tuned within a controlled window. Excessive heating or misadjusted spray conditions may still increase oxidation or compromise adhesion, so the process window is limited.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative gains in thickness and the exact process window for minimizing oxidation remain to be fully defined; variations in feedstock particle size distribution or minor compositional changes may affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct two parallel deposition trials: one using the current thermal-spray process and one using the optimized HVOF process on identical FeCoNiCrAl feedstock. Maintain constant substrate and ambient conditions. Post-deposition, measure the coating thickness, analyze the microstructure and assess oxidation levels using SEM, XRD, and XPS/EDS.
measurements: Coating thickness (in μm) across multiple sample areas
Oxide scale composition and depth profile
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HVOF-deposited coating does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness (for example, less than a 20% improvement over the baseline) or shows increased levels of oxidation or compromised integrity compared to the current process, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.
